questions.statement: A teacher is a person ________ helps students to learn.

options.text: who
options.feedback: Correct! We use "who" to refer to people.

options.text: which
options.feedback: Incorrect. "Which" is for things or animals.

options.text: where
options.feedback: Incorrect. "Where" is for places.

options.text: when
options.feedback: Incorrect. "When" is for time.

questions.explanation:
Las oraciones de relativo (relative clauses) nos permiten dar información extra sobre alguien o algo. Usamos "who" específicamente para personas.

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: This is the book ________ I told you about.

options.text: who
options.feedback: Incorrect. A book is not a person.

options.text: that
options.feedback: Correct! "That" can be used for both people and things in defining relative clauses.

options.text: where
options.feedback: "Where" points to a place, but "this is the book" refers to a thing, not to a location.

options.text: whom
options.feedback: "Whom" is used for people in the object position; the antecedent here is a book, so it cannot take "whom".

questions.explanation:
"That" es un pronombre relativo muy versátil que puede usarse tanto para objetos (cosas) como para personas en oraciones especificativas.

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: The library is a place ________ you can find many books and study in silence.

options.text: which
options.feedback: Incorrect. While a library is a thing, here we refer to it as a location where an action happens.

options.text: where
options.feedback: Correct! "Where" is the relative pronoun for places.

options.text: who
options.feedback: "Who" is used for people, and a library is a place, so it needs the locative relative pronoun.

options.text: that
options.feedback: "That" can join things to clauses, but after "a place" the clause describes a location, which is what "where" does.

questions.explanation:
Cuando nos referimos a un lugar como el sitio donde ocurre una acción, el pronombre relativo adecuado es "where".

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: The condor is a bird ________ lives in the highest parts of the Andes.

options.text: who
options.feedback: Incorrect. "Who" is strictly for humans.

options.text: which
options.feedback: Correct! "Which" is used for animals and inanimate objects.

options.text: where
options.feedback: "Where" marks a place, but the relative pronoun here refers to the condor, which is an animal.

options.text: whose
options.feedback: Incorrect. "Whose" is for possession.

questions.explanation:
Para animales u objetos, el pronombre relativo estándar es "which", aunque también se podría usar "that" en este contexto.

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: That is the student ________ father is a famous scientist.

options.text: who
options.feedback: Incorrect. "Who" doesn't show possession.

options.text: whose
options.feedback: Correct! "Whose" is used to show possession (whose father = el padre del cual).

options.text: which
options.feedback: "Which" introduces a thing, not a person; the clause here describes a student's father.

options.text: whom
options.feedback: "Whom" marks the object of a preposition for people, but possession is expressed with "whose".

questions.explanation:
"Whose" se traduce como "cuyo/a" o "de quien". Se usa para indicar que algo pertenece a la persona o cosa mencionada anteriormente.

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Arepa is a traditional food ________ is made from corn.

options.text: who
options.feedback: "Who" refers to a person, and an arepa is a food, so it cannot be the antecedent of "who".

options.text: where
options.feedback: "Where" marks a place, but the clause describes what the arepa is made from, not where it is.

options.text: that
options.feedback: Correct! Referring to an object (food).

options.text: when
options.feedback: "When" marks a time, and the clause about corn states an ingredient rather than a moment.

questions.explanation:
En definiciones de objetos culturales, usamos "that" o "which" para conectar el nombre del objeto con su descripción o proceso de fabricación.

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: In which sentence can the relative pronoun be **omitted** (deleted)?

options.text: The man who lives next door is a musician.
options.feedback: Incorrect. "Who" is the subject of "lives".

options.text: The movie (that) we watched yesterday was boring.
options.feedback: Correct! "That" is the object (we watched it), so it can be omitted.

options.text: The girl who won the prize is my sister.
options.feedback: Incorrect. "Who" is the subject.

options.text: A hospital is a building where people go when they are sick.
options.feedback: Incorrect. "Where" is rarely omitted this way.

questions.explanation:
En inglés, podemos omitir "who", "which" o "that" solo cuando funcionan como el **objeto** de la oración de relativo (cuando hay otro sujeto después del pronombre).

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement:
"An orphan is a child whose parents are dead."
What information does the relative clause provide?

options.text: It describes where the child lives.
options.feedback: The clause says nothing about where the child lives; it identifies the parents as the ones who are dead.

options.text: It gives essential information to define what an orphan is.
options.feedback: Correct! Without this clause, we don't know which child we mean.

options.text: It is extra information that we can delete without changing the meaning.
options.feedback: Incorrect. It's a defining clause.

options.text: It tells us the name of the child.
options.feedback: The clause never gives a name, so it cannot be telling us who the child is called.

questions.explanation:
Las "defining relative clauses" (oraciones de relativo especificativas) son esenciales para el significado de la oración; sin ellas, el sustantivo principal no queda bien definido.

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement:
Combine these two sentences:
"I lost the watch. My grandmother gave it to me."

options.text: I lost the watch who my grandmother gave to me.
options.feedback: Incorrect. Watch is not a person.

options.text: I lost the watch that my grandmother gave to me.
options.feedback: Correct! "That" connects the object to its origin.

options.text: I lost the watch where my grandmother gave to me.
options.feedback: "Where" marks a place, but the clause explains the origin of the watch, which points to a thing.

options.text: I lost the watch whose my grandmother gave to me.
options.feedback: "Whose" shows possession, and the grandmother gave the watch; she is not claiming to own it beforehand.

questions.explanation:
Para combinar oraciones, reemplazamos el objeto repetido ("it") por un pronombre relativo ("that" o "which") que conecte ambas ideas.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.context: Identifying errors in formal relative clauses.

options.text: The woman with whom I was speaking is my aunt.
options.feedback: Incorrect. This is formal but correct.

options.text: That's the house in which I grew up.
options.feedback: Incorrect. Formal but correct.

options.text: This is the park who I used to play in.
options.feedback: Correct! Error found. "Park" is a place or thing, so "who" is wrong.

options.text: The people whose car was stolen are very sad.
options.feedback: Incorrect. This is correct.

questions.explanation:
El nivel B1 requiere distinguir claramente entre referentes humanos ("who") y no humanos ("which/that") en cualquier estructura, por compleja que sea.

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which description is more precise for a dictionary entry?

options.text: A pen is a thing for writing.
options.feedback: Incorrect. Too simple.

options.text: A pen is an instrument that uses ink to write on paper.
options.feedback: Correct! Precise use of a relative clause to define purpose.

options.text: A pen is who you use to write.
options.feedback: Incorrect. Grammatically wrong.

options.text: Pen is a place where words are.
options.feedback: A pen is an instrument used for writing, not a location, so calling it a place where words are reverses its meaning.

questions.explanation:
El uso de oraciones de relativo es fundamental para crear definiciones precisas y académicas (habilidad evaluada en B1).

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the best way to describe "The Gold Museum" (El Museo del Oro) in Bogotá:
questions.context: Writing a descriptive sentence about a Colombian landmark.

options.text: It is a world-famous museum which houses the largest collection of pre-Hispanic gold work.
options.feedback: Correct! Uses a relative clause to provide essential and impressive information.

options.text: It is a place who has many golden things for people.
options.feedback: Incorrect. "Who" is for people, not places.

options.text: It is the building where gold was invented long ago.
options.feedback: Incorrect. Gold is a natural element, not "invented" in a museum.

options.text: It is a museum that it is near the city center.
options.feedback: Incorrect. Doubling the subject (that it is) is a common error.

questions.explanation: La creación de descripciones complejas requiere el uso de pronombres relativos adecuados y evitar errores comunes como la redundancia del sujeto ("that it is").
